body:
CTRL+C stops the current execution.
So, if you press CTRL+C while starship is running, you stop it from returning the nice prompt you expect. This is the expected behavior.
Your sporadically disappearing prompt is more of a concern.

What I am trying to say is that CTRL+C  is not the appropriate way to reproduce the issue you are seeing.

More about the locations you are navigating to would be interesting (i.e. git repos? Rust dirs? etc..)?

For what it is worth, I'm using starship on W10 with Powershell 7 and am not seeing this issue.

I just used `CTRL+C` because it was the fastest way to get a bunch of new prompts, but it reproduces with any command. Here's another example with `ls` in a completely empty directory:

```powershell
PowerShell 7.0.0
Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

https://aka.ms/powershell
Type 'help' to get help.

PS>mkdir empty


    Directory: C:\Users\Chris

Mode                 LastWriteTime         Length Name
----                 -------------         ------ ----
d----          07.05.2020    08:34                empty

PS>cd empty

~/empty
❯ ls

~/empty
❯ ls
PS>ls
PS>ls

~/empty
❯ ls
PS>
```
I just noticed that the issue did not stem from the 0.41.0 update, so it must have been something in my environment that changed. I'll investigate what exactly might have changed to cause this.
When the prompt breaks what does `(Get-Command prompt).Definition` return?

```
PS>(Get-Command prompt).Definition

    $out = $null
    # @ makes sure the result is an array even if single or no values are returned
    $jobs = @(Get-Job | Where-Object { $_.State -eq 'Running' }).Count

    if ($lastCmd = Get-History -Count 1) {
        $duration = [math]::Round(($lastCmd.EndExecutionTime - $lastCmd.StartExecutionTime).TotalMilliseconds)
        # & ensures the path is interpreted as something to execute
        $out = @(&"C:\Users\Chris\.cargo\bin\starship.exe" prompt "--path=$PWD" --status=$lastexitcode --jobs=$jobs --cmd-duration=$duration)
    } else {
        $out = @(&"C:\Users\Chris\.cargo\bin\starship.exe" prompt "--path=$PWD" --status=$lastexitcode --jobs=$jobs)
    }

    # Convert stdout (array of lines) to expected return type string
    # `n is an escaped newline
    $out -join "`n"

PS>
```

Manually calling the command with `RUST_LOG` set to `trace` doesn't produce any additional output:

```
PS>$jobs = @(Get-Job | Where-Object { $_.State -eq 'Running' }).Count
PS>$env:RUST_LOG="trace"
PS>C:\Users\Chris\.cargo\bin\starship.exe prompt "--path=$PWD" --status=$lastexitcode --jobs=$jobs
PS>
```

I think I pinpointed the issues.

I must have adjusted my `.cargo/config` in the time between updates, and it's this combination of rustflags that causes the issue to appear:

```toml
[build]
rustflags=[
	"-Clinker-flavor=lld-link",
	"-Ctarget-cpu=sandybridge",	
]
```

Interestingly, each rustflag individually does *not* result in this issue. That is, with `"-Ctarget-cpu=sandybridge"` on its own it works reliably, as well as with `"-Clinker-flavor=lld-link"` on its own. 

So since this is an environment issue (or upstream issue?), feel free to close this. It would still be interesting to find out why this combination of rustflags breaks starship in this way. Since configuring it I've not once encountered an issue like this in any other crate or application compiled with cargo.
(Except, now that I noticed that this particular combination of rustflags breaks some things, I figured out it also caused the `STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION` in rustc I saw when trying to compile the `sd` crate. I might file an issue upstream.)

> Manually calling the command with RUST_LOG set to trace doesn't produce any additional output

Please try calling the command with `RUST_LOG` set to `starship=trace`.
